papers.title: Phonology-Aware Speaker Extraction Frontend for Audio LLMs
papers.abstract: Target speaker extraction (TSE) is a key frontend for enabling audio large language models (LLMs) to recognize and understand a designated speaker in overlapping speech. However, multilingual mixtures exhibit heterogeneous extraction demands, causing fixed-depth systems to either under-process challenging inputs or waste computation on inputs that have already converged. Existing TSE frontends generally apply uniform computation, while Audio-LLM adaptation methods neither explicitly model language-conditioned extraction demands nor preserve plug-and-play compatibility with frozen downstream models. We therefore propose LATTE, a lightweight 5.2M-parameter frontend that combines an acoustic Difficulty Estimator, a task-adaptive phonology-informed prior learned from multi-depth TSE gains, and an Adaptive Hourglass Extractor to route each mixture without requiring language identity at inference. On PolyExtract, LATTE achieves a macro SI-SNRi of 15.07 dB at 0.30 GFLOPs, retaining performance within 0.09 dB of a 0.53-GFLOP fixed-depth model while reducing computation by 43.4%, and lowers the average WER from 16.8% to 14.6% relative to TF-GridNet. By jointly modeling sample-level extraction demands and phonological structure, LATTE provides a practical framework for quality-aware, compute-efficient multilingual TSE and offers a scalable path toward robust Audio-LLM deployment.

papers.title: VoTSpeech: Decoupling Voice Design from Speech Generation in Instruction-Following TTS
papers.abstract: Instruction-following text-to-speech (TTS) typically leaves voice design implicit, as conventional speaker embeddings encode reference audio rather than text-driven targets. We propose VoTSpeech, which decouples voice design from speech generation via an explicit intermediate voice latent. Built on a shared language model backbone, VoTSpeech first predicts a continuous voice latent from text instructions using a flow-based module. This latent serves as a shared condition for both the language model and the Acoustic DiT, guiding autoregressive sequence modeling and acoustic latent generation, respectively, before an audio VAE decoder converts the acoustic latents into waveforms. To capture speaker identity and complementary acoustic nuances, the voice latent is jointly supervised by speaker embeddings and temporally pooled audio VAE features. With task-specific adaptation, VoTSpeech performs strongly on InstructTTSEval-ZH, demonstrating competitive capabilities against strong open-source models while maintaining high naturalness. These results confirm that explicit voice latent design and its conditioning interface effectively empower text-driven voice design for controllable speech synthesis. Code, model, and audio samples are available at https://github.com/ywbn/VoTSpeech .

papers.title: AudioTETRIS: Token Elimination via Transitional Importance Signals for Efficient Audio LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) achieve strong performance on speech-text tasks, but standard audio encoders produce hundreds of tokens for even short audio clips. Because self-attention scales quadratically in sequence length, this inflates inference-time compute substantially. Current training-free token compression methods prune or merge tokens based solely on coarse attention or feature similarity. However, treating audio tokens as generic, isotropic features smooths over spectral transitions, destroying fine-grained phonetic transitions essential for decoding speech. In contrast, speech signals exhibit highly structured temporal patterns where information density peaks at acoustic transitions. We propose AudioTETRIS, a training-free, two-stage framework that uses the audio encoder's representation geometry as an acoustic prior for token importance before applying attention-based compression. Instead of discarding encoder structure after the encoding stage, AudioTETRIS propagates this prior directly into the LLM decoder to compute a per-token fused score. This score drives progressive top-$k$ token selection across decoder layers without requiring additional training or auxiliary models. Evaluated on Qwen2-Audio-7B, Phi-4-Multimodal, and Audio Flamingo 3, AudioTETRIS retains near-uncompressed performance on several speech tasks using only 25% of audio tokens, matches or surpasses full-token accuracy at moderate compression rates, and consistently outperforms existing training-free baselines.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: audio language model, audio llm

papers.title: Training a Compact, Strong, and Realistic Text-to-Speech Model
papers.abstract: Text-to-speech (TTS) systems are conventionally optimized for intelligibility and speaker similarity. However, neither objective captures the prosodic detail that distinguishes human performances from synthetic speech, leaving a realism gap that larger models and higher-quality data can narrow but not close. In the absence of an objective that directly targets this gap, realism remains a persistent challenge in TTS. We present Audio8-TTS, a compact 0.6B-parameter model for zero-shot voice cloning that achieves state-of-the-art performance in intelligibility and speaker similarity, with particularly strong results in perceptual naturalness. To align the training signal with human perception rather than signal-level fidelity, we construct a quality ladder from widely used open-source TTS systems and train a realism critic to assess generated speech against matched human recordings of the same sentences. An identity-erasure objective discourages the critic from relying on generator fingerprints. We train the model in three stages: multilingual supervised fine-tuning; group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with word error rate (WER) and speaker similarity (SIM) rewards; and GRPO guided by the realism critic. The final stage improves perceived prosodic naturalness and speaker similarity while preserving WER performance.

papers.title: AphaVoice: Text-to-Speech Model for Aphasia Patient Simulation
papers.abstract: While language therapy is the primary treatment for post-stroke aphasia, limited clinical resources often restrict patient access to proper care. Addressing this gap requires reliable training simulations for medical professionals. However, current AI efforts focus almost exclusively on speech processing, leaving speech generation largely unexplored. This study introduces AphaVoice, a novel text-to-speech (TTS) framework explicitly engineered to synthesize highly realistic aphasic speech. Evaluated against state-of-the-art TTS systems, AphaVoice demonstrates a superior ability to capture the clinical feature of dysfluency, outperforming existing models in temporal metrics while consistently maintaining speaker identity. By leveraging latent space shifting, the model also supports multi-speaker generation without sacrificing phonetic realism. Ultimately, AphaVoice provides a scalable, high-fidelity tool for medical training and clinical simulation related to aphasia.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: speech generation, text-to-speech

papers.title: Missing Melodies: AI Music Generation and Its “Nearly” Complete Omission of the Global South
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI have sparked renewed interest and expanded possibilities for music generation. However, the performance and versatility of these systems across musical genres are heavily influenced by the availability of training data. We conducted an extensive analysis of over one million hours of audio datasets used in AI music generation research, and manually reviewed more than 200 papers from eleven prominent AI and music conferences and organizations to identify a critical gap in the fair representation and inclusion of the musical genres of the Global South in AI research. Our findings reveal a stark imbalance: approximately 86% of the total dataset hours and over 88% of researchers focus primarily on music from the Global North. However, around 40% of these datasets include some form of non-Western music, and genres from the Global South account for only 14.6% of the data. Furthermore, approximately 51% of the papers surveyed concentrate on symbolic music generation, a method that often fails to capture the cultural nuances inherent in music from regions such as South Asia, the Middle East, and Africa. As AI increasingly shapes the creation and dissemination of music, the significant underrepresentation of music genres in datasets and research presents a serious threat to global musical diversity, including evaluating music generation models, economic disparities, and reinforcing biases in generative music models. We also propose some important steps to mitigate these risks and foster a more inclusive future for AI-driven music generation.

papers.title: Personalization Without Stereotyping: Do Speech LLMs Know When to Turn a Deaf Ear?
papers.abstract: Recent speech LLMs can leverage rich paralinguistic cues, enabling more complex and personalized interactions. However, little work investigates how this sensitivity can lead to stereotyping, and existing evaluations largely measure demographic disparities without distinguishing beneficial personalization from stereotypical behavior. We introduce BASIS-Bench, a benchmark designed to disentangle these two aspects through three axes: (1) demographic robustness, measuring disparities in content-based tasks across speakers and demographic classification capabilities; (2) stereotypical bias, measuring whether perceived demographic cues trigger unprompted stereotypical behavior; and (3) personalization, measuring whether models can tailor responses to demographic characteristics when explicitly requested. We evaluate eight recent speech LLMs and find that, despite often recognizing demographic cues, most fail to translate them into appropriate personalization. Explicit demographic labels improve personalization but also amplify stereotypical associations already present in the textual backbones. These findings highlight the need to train speech LLMs not only to perceive demographic cues, but to learn when they should shape their responses.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: speech llm

papers.title: Frontend-Assisted Large Audio-Language Models for SLT2026 SmartGlasses Challenge
papers.abstract: This paper describes our systems for the Track 1 time-stamped speaker-attributed ASR task of the SmartGlasses Challenge. To handle overlapping speech, background noise and far-field conditions in two-person conversations, we employ SoulX-Transcriber, a multimodal large language model that takes full-length audio as input and generates structured transcriptions. In addition, we investigate the effect of speech frontend processing, including a rule-based Guided Source Separation method and a data-driven speech separation model, both of which improve performance on the validation set. Considering inference stability, our final submission uses the fine-tuned SoulX-Transcriber system, achieving a tcpCER of 6.22 on the test set.

papers.title: Does Location Matter? A Black-Box Causal Audit Reveals Model-Dependent Audio Grounding in LALM Hallucination
papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) frequently exhibit object hallucination, affirming absent sounds. The dominant mitigation, Audio-Aware Decoding (AAD), contrasts logits under real audio against an all-zero"blank"waveform, flagged by prior review as out-of-distribution. We introduce a black-box causal test that isolates the claimed evidence itself: localize a claim's evidence region via CLAP similarity, remove it by spectral gating, and compare against a random-window control across a 2x2x2 grid on three LALMs. On Qwen2-Audio-7B, localized ablation's raw AUROC trails blank's (0.613 vs. 0.721); this is a duration confound, not a localization failure, since blank removes the entire clip versus the grid's 2-4 s. Holding duration fixed, localization beats random removal at every cell on both models. Raw detection value remains model-dependent, especially on Audio Flamingo 3. The same evidence corrects decoding: contrastive decoding combining blank and language-prior contrasts, gated and ensembled, raises Qwen2-Audio accuracy from 57.1% to 71.9%, beating AAD alone. A unified causal-grounding profile does not transfer between models, indicating different grounding regimes. The source code and a detailed report of our findings, including identified limitations, are available at https://github.com/khalooei/causa.

papers.title: What Do Audio-Language Judges of Generated Music Listen For? Four Probes with Controls from Expert Ratings
papers.abstract: Open audio-language models are used as judges of generated music: given a clip and its text prompt, the model rates the clip, and the judge is validated by how well its ratings correlate with expert ratings. The correlation does not show what the judge responds to: the music, the text prompt, or the way the question is asked. We propose four probes that test each of these, three of them read against a control computed from the human ratings: removing the audio, replacing the clip with another model's clip for the same prompt, swapping the order of two clips in pairwise judging, and rewording the instruction. We apply them to five open judges on all 2,748 clips of MusicEval, and the last two to the SongEval songs. Without audio, no judge exceeds what the prompt alone predicts from the human ratings, and for prompt alignment every judge falls below it. With audio, every judge follows the clip it hears when rating prompt alignment, two do when rating musical quality, and the strongest judge's quality score tracks the experts'alignment rating more than their quality rating. The pairwise verdicts of the four smaller judges follow the position of a clip in the pair (its slot) rather than its quality on both rating sets. For musical quality, rewording the instruction moves the correlation of most judges as much as changing the judge. MusicEval's prompt assignment bounds any prompt-only judge at the model level. We recommend reporting the four probes with every music judge.

## Model Description

**Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0** is an audio-capable version of [Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1).
The model was developed by [LINAGORA](https://linagora.com) and
the [OpenLLM-France](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France) consortium, as part of the OpenLLM France project funded by
[BPI France](https://www.bpifrance.fr/) under the France 2030 program.

The training of Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0 was conducted on the Jean Zay supercomputer managed by [IDRIS](http://www.idris.fr/docs/idris/missions),
using the [NVIDIA NeMo Speech](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech) toolkit.
The model was trained on various tasks and types of audio, including ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition), AST (Automatic Speech Translation), QA (Question Answering), Sound (Question Answering and Captioning), Music (Question Answering and Captioning) and more.

### Bias, Risks, and Limitations

- Inherits the limitations of the base [Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1)
  language model: it can struggle with math word problems, is susceptible to hallucination, and its
  context window is limited to 16,384 tokens.
<!-- - The audio encoder and its front-end were entirely frozen during training, so audio understanding is bounded by what
  Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 already hears: the model cannot learn to compensate for acoustic conditions the
  encoder itself handles poorly. -->
- Language coverage is uneven. French and English make up most of the training mix and are the only languages seen on every task. German, Spanish and Italian were seen in training for ASR, AST and spoken QA. Portuguese, Dutch and Arabic for ASR and AST only.
- Arabic is the weakest language: the frozen Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 encoder was not trained on Arabic,
  so the model is clearly less reliable there (FLEURS WER ~30%).
<!-- - LoRA fine-tuning only touches attention projections in the LLM; no additional audio-specific safety or
  refusal tuning was performed beyond what the base LLM already has. -->

### Recommendations

- Speech, sound and music understanding: (summarization, captioning, sound/music QA, conversation):
  best in French and English, the only languages the model was trained on for these tasks.
- Transcription (ASR) and translation (AST): supported in French, English, German, Spanish,
  Italian, Portuguese and Dutch. For production ASR/AST pipelines, a dedicated model may still
  perform better.
- Spoken question answering: mainly supported in French and English. German, Spanish and
  Italian are also supported, but with far less training data.
- Other languages and tasks: outside French and English, evaluate the model on your own data
  before relying on it, especially for a task the model was not trained on in that language.
- Up-to-date or domain-specific knowledge: as with the base LLM, pair the model with a RAG
  pipeline.

## Training details

### Training data

Trained on the [OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training-Dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training-Dataset),
a large multilingual, multi-task collection of audio–text conversations comprising: ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition),
AST (Automatic Speech Translation), spoken question answering, summarization, diarization, temporal localization,
speaker/gender/age/emotion/language recognition, and music/sound captioning and QA (Question Answering).

### Instruction template

Same chat template as the base LLM (inspired by Qwen3), extended with an `<|audio|>` locator tag:
wherever `<|audio|>` appears in a turn, the corresponding audio segment is encoded and its embeddings
replace the tag before the sequence reaches the LLM. Conversations can carry several audio clips and mix
audio-only, text-only, and audio+text turns within the same dialogue (see the
[dataset card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training-Dataset) for example
conversations).

### Training Procedure

| Component | Details |
|---|---|
| **Audio encoder** | [Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3) Conformer encoder, frozen |
| **RoTE** | Applied between audio encoder and audio adapter. θ=1200, rotary fraction=0.2. Inspired by [Goel et al., 2024, OMCAT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.12109).|
| **Audio adapter** | Linear projection into the LLM embedding space (1024 -> 4096) |
| **LLM** | [Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1), adapted with LoRA (on `q_proj`/`v_proj`, `up_proj`, `down_proj`, r=64, α=64) |
| **Trainable params** | 82.1M / ~8.2B (1.0%) |
| **Optimizer** | AdamW (β=(0.9, 0.98), weight decay 0.001) |
| **LR schedule** | Cosine annealing (max LR 2e-4, min LR 1e-6, 500 warmup steps) |
| **Batching** | Dynamic, bucketed by audio duration (27 buckets) |
| **Steps** | 100,000 |
| **Gradient clipping** | 1.0 |
| **Strategy** | FSDP2 (full sharding), activation checkpointing on the LLM (to allow for long sequences), 1 node × 4 H100 |
| **Precision** | bf16 |

The model was trained for 100k steps and drew from a weighted, randomly-ordered, sharded mix of that dataset,
bucketed by duration into 27 buckets (up to 1,200s / 16,384 audio-equivalent tokens per example) with a
matching dynamic batch size per bucket (238 down to 1).

Validation covered CommonVoice ASR (fr/en/ar),
Multilingual TEDx speech translation (fr→en), spoken QA (SLUE-SQA-5, VoxPopuli-QA, en/fr), and audio/music
captioning (AudioCaps, MusicCaps).

The training code and configs are available in the [Luciole-Audio-Training repository](https://github.com/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training). Training used an updated version of [NeMo/Speech 3.1](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech) which can be found in our [NeMo/Speech fork](https://github.com/linagora-labs/NeMo/tree/luciole_speech.3.1.0-rc0).

## Evaluation

To evaluate our models and compare them with other open-weight Audio LLMs, we used [our fork of AudioBench](https://github.com/OpenLLM-France/AudioBench). We used a combination of datasets from AudioBench and datasets available in [our HF audio evaluation repository](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Evaluation-Dataset). You can find the full details and results on [our AudioBench leaderboard](https://openllm-france.github.io/AudioBench/).

## Using the model

### With vLLM

The exported checkpoint's `config.json` declares `"model_type": "nemo_speechlm"` and
`"architectures": ["NeMoSpeechLMForConditionalGeneration"]`. Both are registered with vLLM by the SALM
plugin that ships inside `nemo-toolkit`
([`nemo.collections.speechlm2.vllm.salm`](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech/tree/main/nemo/collections/speechlm2/vllm/salm))
via the `vllm.general_plugins` entry point:

```toml
[project.entry-points."vllm.general_plugins"]
nemo_speechlm = "nemo.collections.speechlm2.vllm.salm:register"
```

vLLM auto-discovers this plugin at startup as soon as `nemo-toolkit` and `vllm` are installed in the same
environment. The plugin merges the
LoRA adapters into the LLM backbone on load and runs the frozen Parakeet encoder + connector to turn each
`<|audio|>` tag into the right number of audio-embedding slots before generation.

**Install using uv**

```bash
uv venv .venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

uv pip install "nemo-toolkit[speechlm2,tts] @ git+https://github.com/linagora-labs/NeMo.git@luciole-1b-vllm-nemotron-fix"
uv pip install vllm==0.28.0
uv pip install "numpy<=2.4"
```

**Serve**

```bash
vllm serve OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0 \
    --max-model-len 16384
```

**Query** (OpenAI-compatible chat API, audio sent as base64):

```python
import base64
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY")

with open("sample.wav", "rb") as f:   # 16 kHz mono
    audio_b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode()

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {"type": "text", "text": "Transcris cet audio en français : <|audio|>"},
                {"type": "input_audio", "input_audio": {"data": audio_b64, "format": "wav"}},
            ],
        }
    ],
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

The `<|audio|>` placeholder is the same `audio_locator_tag` used during training: put it in the text
wherever the audio should be attended to; the plugin expands it automatically. Audio must be 16 kHz mono;
the encoder supports chunked processing for long-form audio (well beyond the durations seen in training).

### With NeMo

The checkpoint can also be loaded directly with NeMo's `SALM` class
([`nemo.collections.speechlm2.models.salm`](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech/blob/main/nemo/collections/speechlm2/models/salm.py)).

**Install**

```bash
uv venv .venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

uv pip install "nemo-toolkit[speechlm2,tts] @ git+https://github.com/linagora-labs/NeMo.git@luciole-1b-vllm-nemotron-fix"
```

**Load and generate:**

```python
import torch
from nemo.collections.speechlm2 import SALM

model = SALM.from_pretrained("OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0")  # or a local checkpoint directory
model = model.eval().to(torch.bfloat16).to("cuda")

# High-level API: pass the audio file path(s) directly in the prompt, next to the
# `<|audio|>` placeholder; SALM loads and resamples the audio for you.
answer_ids = model.generate(
    prompts=[
        [
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": f"Transcris cet audio en français : {model.audio_locator_tag}",
                "audio": ["sample.wav"],
            }
        ]
    ],
    max_new_tokens=256,
)
print(model.tokenizer.ids_to_text(answer_ids[0].tolist()))
```

A prompt can carry several turns and several audio clips (one `<|audio|>` tag per clip, in order).

### Example prompts for each task

- ASR: 
  - `Make a word-for-word transcription in English of the spoken content.`
  - `Fais une transcription mot pour mot en français du contenu parlé.`
- QA: `Listen to the audio and answer the question.`
- AST: `Translate this file into French.`
- Diarization: 
  - `Provide a time-stamped, speaker-attributed transcript of this audio.`
  - `Transcris et diarise cet enregistrement, avec les horodatages de chaque tour.`

# MOSS-Music-8B-Instruct, MLX 8-bit

[OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Music-8B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Music-8B-Instruct) converted to
[MLX](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx) and quantized to 8 bits, for a Mac with 24 GB of memory or more. It listens to music and answers
questions about it in text. A community conversion: the model is the OpenMOSS Team's, and so is the credit.

It was made to be the local "ears" of [Trainspotting Suite](https://github.com/remy-st/trainspotting-suite), where it
hears every track sixteen bars at a time and fills in a form (who is singing and how, what the synth sounds like, the
words, the mood). There, `python -m djkit ears fetch` downloads it and nothing else needs setting up.

The other size: [5-bit](https://huggingface.co/FractalSurfer/MOSS-Music-8B-Instruct-mlx-5bit)

# DuplexJev-4B

> **Archived.** Superseded by [DuplexJev-4B-Para](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B-Para). This is the version before the turn-taking upgrade (paper model, total 78.6); 4B-Para scores 82.5. This repository stays online for existing users and paper reproducibility, but is no longer updated.

📄 Paper: [arXiv:2610.02638](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02638) · Code: [github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev)

**Built on [Qwen3-4B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-4B) + the [Qwen3-ASR-0.6B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-0.6B) audio encoder.**

DuplexJev reads typed, closed-set decisions from speech (*has the user finished? which filler fits? who is speaking,
in what mood?*) as a **single-token distribution** of a frozen LLM: zero decode steps, many questions about the same
clip in parallel. This repository is the **complete model** (encoder + trained connector + LLM, 4.2 B parameters, bf16)
and runs on [vLLM](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm) with a small plugin.

| | |
|---|---|
| Audio encoder (frozen) | Qwen3-ASR-0.6B encoder, 12.5 frames/s |
| Connector (trained, 12.6 M) | 2 frames stacked → 6.25 audio tokens/s → SwiGLU MLP → LLM width |
| LLM (frozen) | Qwen3-4B, used without thinking |
| Training | content alignment (transcript distillation), then turn-taking + gender + emotion under the mixed objective (2026-10-01 update) |
| Try it online | [api.adventists.cn/duplexjev](https://api.adventists.cn/duplexjev/) (web demo and trial API, this model) |

## Serve with vLLM

```bash
pip install "vllm[audio]>=0.29" duplexjev-vllm
vllm serve adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B --max-model-len 4096
```

`duplexjev-vllm` registers the model with vLLM (Qwen3-ASR encoder + connector; the LLM runs on vLLM's own Qwen3
kernels). Tested with vLLM 0.29 on one GPU; the model needs about 8 GB plus KV cache.

Each question is one chat request with `max_tokens=1`: list the options under letters and read the log-probabilities
of the letters. Requests about the same clip share the prompt prefix (chat header + audio), which vLLM's prefix cache
computes once. A ready-made client (`openai` + standard library only) is
[`examples/vllm_client.py`](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/examples/vllm_client.py):

```python
from vllm_client import DuplexJevClient

dj = DuplexJevClient("http://localhost:8000/v1")
dj.decide(open("call.wav", "rb").read(), {
    "turn":    ("Has the user finished speaking?", ["finished", "not finished"]),
    "gender":  ("What is the perceived gender of the speaker?", ["female", "male"]),
    "emotion": ("What is the speaker's emotional state?", ["neutral", "happy", "angry", "sad"]),
})
# {'turn': {'answer': 'finished', 'confidence': 0.88, 'probs': {...}}, 'gender': {...}, 'emotion': {...}}
```

The prompt it sends, which is the format the connector was trained on:

```
The user said: <|audio|>

Question: What is the perceived gender of the speaker?

Options:
A. female
B. male

Answer with only the letter of the correct option.
```

For Chinese speech ask in Chinese: `用户说：<|audio|>`, `问题：…`, `选项：`, `请只回答正确选项的字母。`
Send the audio as an `input_audio` part next to that text; restrict the answer with `allowed_token_ids` (the letter
tokens) and set `logprobs=True`. The chat template turns thinking off by default.

## Results

Paper protocol (single-token readout; % correct):

| version | qa100 | ZJU-ML | Easy-Turn | gender (800) | emotion (800, 4-way) | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **current (2026-10-01)** | 74 | 50 | **78.1**\* | 88.6 | 91.2 | **78.6** |
| first release (2026-09-28, in the repo history) | 72 | 51 | 60.2 | 89.4 | 91.9 | 75.9 |

\* The current version's decision stage includes the Easy-Turn **training** split (disjoint from the 800-item test set,
different wording), so Easy-Turn is in-domain for it. Total = mean of main language (qa100, ZJU-ML, Easy-Turn) and
paralinguistics (gender, emotion).

Served by vLLM 0.29 with `duplexjev-vllm`, questions in the wording of the client above: qa100 74, ZJU-ML 52,
Easy-Turn 77.9, gender 87.8, emotion 86.0. One decision event (8 questions about one clip) takes about 80 ms on a
shared H100.

qa100: 100 bilingual spoken multiple-choice questions ([`adventists-ai/qa100`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/adventists-ai/qa100)).
ZJU-ML: main-language part of the ZJU audio benchmark v2.0.0. Easy-Turn: 800-item four-way turn-state test set
(see the [GitHub README](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev#6-benchmarks) for the reference).
Gender: 800 real utterances (AISHELL-1, LibriSpeech). Emotion: 800 utterances (ESD, CREMA-D).

## Limitations

- Evaluated on short read or acted speech; not on streaming input.
- Spoken factual QA is much weaker than in [DuplexJev-32B](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B).
- Emotion labels come from acted corpora; do not use the outputs to make decisions about individuals.

family: strongest English reasoning of the LLMs we tested, Apache-2.0 base.

DuplexJev reads typed, closed-set decisions from speech (*has the user finished? who is speaking, in what mood?*) as a
**single-token distribution** of the LLM: zero decode steps, many questions about the same clip in parallel. This
repository is the **complete model** (encoder + trained connector + LLM, bf16, about 58 GB) and runs on
[vLLM](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm) with a small plugin.

| | |
|---|---|
| Audio encoder (frozen) | Qwen3-ASR-0.6B encoder, 12.5 frames/s |
| Connector (trained) | 2 frames stacked → 6.25 audio tokens/s → SwiGLU MLP → LLM width; audio embeddings ×3 and wrapped in Gemma's native `<\|audio> … <audio\|>` markers |
| LLM | Gemma-4-31B-it text model. **Unlike DuplexJev-32B / 4B, the LLM is not frozen**: a LoRA (r 16, α 32, q/k/v/o) was trained in the paralinguistic stage and merged into the weights |
| Training | content alignment (transcript distillation, LLM frozen) → LoRA content warm-up → gender + emotion with LoRA under the mixed objective (CE on decisions, KL on content) |
| Inputs | audio + text. Gemma's vision tower is not included. |

## Serve with vLLM

```bash
pip install "vllm[audio]>=0.29" "duplexjev-vllm>=0.2.0"
vllm serve adventists-ai/DuplexJev-Gemma-31B --max-model-len 4096
```

One 80 GB GPU is enough (or `--tensor-parallel-size 2`). `duplexjev-vllm` ≥ 0.2.0 registers
`DuplexJevGemmaForConditionalGeneration` (Qwen3-ASR encoder + connector + ×3 scale + audio markers; the LLM runs on
vLLM's own Gemma kernels). The placeholder in prompts stays `<|audio|>`; the plugin expands it.

Each question is one chat request with `max_tokens=1`: list the options under letters and read the log-probabilities
of the letters. A ready-made client is
[`examples/vllm_client.py`](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/examples/vllm_client.py):

```python
from vllm_client import DuplexJevClient

dj = DuplexJevClient("http://localhost:8000/v1")
dj.decide(open("call.wav", "rb").read(), {
    "gender":  ("What is the perceived gender of the speaker?", ["female", "male"]),
    "emotion": ("What is the speaker's emotional state?", ["neutral", "happy", "angry", "sad"]),
})
```

The prompt format the connector was trained on:

```
The user said: <|audio|>

Question: What is the perceived gender of the speaker?

Options:
A. female
B. male

Answer with only the letter of the correct option.
```

For Chinese speech ask in Chinese: `用户说：<|audio|>`, `问题：…`, `选项：`, `请只回答正确选项的字母。`

## Results

Served by vLLM 0.29 with `duplexjev-vllm` 0.2.0, questions in the training wording above (one H200, bf16; % correct):

| model | qa100 | ZJU-ML | Easy-Turn | gender | emotion |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **DuplexJev-Gemma-31B** (this repo) | **97** | 87 | 68.0\* | **94.4** | 90.6 |
| [DuplexJev-32B](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B) | 94 | **88** | **79.4** | 89.8 | 89.9 |
| [DuplexJev-4B](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B) | 77 | 49 | 60.0 | 87.9 | 90.9 |

\* No turn-taking data was used for this model; Easy-Turn is zero-shot here (DuplexJev-32B saw the Easy-Turn
training split).

**Wording sensitivity.** With a question wording that differs from training (our paper-protocol evaluation script),
this model scores qa100 96, ZJU-ML 84, but gender 78.5 and emotion 60.9. The DuplexJev-32B connector (frozen LLM)
is much less sensitive to wording. Use the prompt format above.

qa100: 100 bilingual spoken multiple-choice questions ([`adventists-ai/qa100`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/adventists-ai/qa100)).
ZJU-ML: main-language part of the ZJU audio benchmark v2.0.0. Easy-Turn: 800-item four-way turn-state test set.
Gender: 800 real utterances (AISHELL-1, LibriSpeech). Emotion: 800 utterances (ESD, CREMA-D).

## Limitations

- Evaluated on short read or acted speech; not on streaming input.
- Paralinguistic accuracy depends on prompt wording (see above).
- No turn-taking training yet; prefer DuplexJev-32B for end-of-turn decisions.
- Emotion labels come from acted corpora; do not use the outputs to make decisions about individuals.

# DuplexJev-4B-Turn

> **Archived.** Superseded by [DuplexJev-4B-Para](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B-Para). 4B-Para keeps the same prompts and plugin and adds non-verbal sounds, speaking style, speaker, stress and normal conversation (total 82.5 vs 80.0). For live end-of-turn on a small GPU, use [DuplexJev-4B-Para-LiveTurn](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B-Para-LiveTurn). This repository stays online for existing users and paper reproducibility, but is no longer updated.

📄 Paper: [arXiv:2610.02638](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02638) · Code: [github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev)

**[DuplexJev-4B](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B) with a turn-taking upgrade.** Same size, same

while spoken QA, gender and emotion stay where they were.

DuplexJev reads typed, closed-set decisions from speech as a **single-token distribution** of the LLM: zero decode
steps, many questions about the same clip in parallel. This repository is the complete model (Qwen3-ASR-0.6B encoder
+ connector + Qwen3-4B, 4.2 B parameters, bf16).

## What changed

Starting from DuplexJev-4B we trained the connector together with a small **LoRA on the LLM** (rank 16 on q/k/v/o,
0.6 % of the parameters; merged into the weights here) on 110 k turn-taking questions rewritten from public
corpora, mixed with the original content and paralinguistic data:

| source | clips | what it teaches |
|---|---:|---|
| Easy-Turn training set (synthetic + real) | 44 k | Chinese: finished / unfinished / backchannel / "wait" |
| SmoothConv | 30 k | Chinese multi-party conversation with turn labels, with text history |
| otoSpeech + DualTurn frame labels | 12.5 k | English two-channel conversation: end of turn, pause, backchannel, interruption |
| DuplexGen Spoken | 14 k | English human–AI dialogues with text history |
| MUSAN noise, distant background voices | 9 k | sounds the assistant should ignore |

Most questions give the **system state** (the assistant is speaking / idle) and ask for an action
(keep talking / stop and listen; reply / keep waiting); the rest ask for the user's turn state.

## Results

| | qa100 | ZJU-ML | gender | emotion | VoiceBench OBQA / MMSU | Easy-Turn | CoDeTT zh / en | TurnBench-dev clips† |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| DuplexJev-4B | 74 | 50 | 88.6 | 91.2 | 47.3 / 41.3 | 78.1 | 62.0 / 53.5 | 49.4 |
| **DuplexJev-4B-Turn** | 74 | 52 | 89.4 | 92.0 | 46.4 / 41.7 | **92.5** | **67.0 / 68.6** | **87.3** |

Paper protocol (single-token readout, PyTorch), % correct. Through vLLM with `duplexjev-vllm` in the client wording:
qa100 77, ZJU-ML 49, gender 87.0, emotion 88.4, Easy-Turn 92.8.

- **Easy-Turn**: 800-item four-way turn-state test set; the training mix contains the Easy-Turn training split
  (disjoint from the test set), so this score is in-domain.
- **CoDeTT** (arXiv 2603.25434): 18 k items, system state given, four actions averaged; zero-shot (no CoDeTT data
  in training). Our protocol: current utterance as audio, no history. For reference, published results: GPT-4o-audio
  66.6 / 71.9, Qwen3-Omni 70.4 / 70.9.
- † **TurnBench-dev clips**: our own clip-level protocol on the TurnBench development conversations (the official test
  labels are withheld): end of turn, pause inside a turn, backchannel, floor-taking interruption, noise / channel
  bleed; mean of four action accuracies. Not comparable with the official TurnBench leaderboard.
- Weakest remaining case: a pause in the middle of a long turn (the model takes the turn too early about half the time).

```bash

vllm serve adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B-Turn --max-model-len 4096
```

Prompt format, client and decision tables are the same as for
[DuplexJev-4B](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B); see

# DuplexJev-4B-Para-LiveTurn

📄 Paper: [arXiv:2610.02638](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02638) · Code: [github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev) · Plugins: [`pipecat-duplexjev`](https://pypi.org/project/pipecat-duplexjev/), [`livekit-plugins-duplexjev`](https://pypi.org/project/livekit-plugins-duplexjev/)

**The 4B DuplexJev tuned for live end-of-turn: is the user done, right after they go quiet?** A turn-taking
variant of [DuplexJev-4B-Para](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B-Para) v1.1, which stays the general 4B.

Same recipe as [DuplexJev-32B-Para v1.2](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Para): the 4B-Para v1.1 mix
plus accent data and pause-level turn-taking data, one rank-16 LoRA, 4,000 steps, merged. Qwen3-ASR-0.6B encoder +
connector + Qwen3-4B, 4.2 B parameters, bf16, ~10 GB GPU memory.

**Which 4B to pick.**
- **This one** for a voice agent's end-of-turn on a small GPU (LiveKit / Pipecat plugins).
- **[4B-Para](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B-Para)** for everything else (stress, non-verbal sounds,
  spoken QA, chat): it is a few points better there, see Limitations.
- **[32B-Para](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Para)** v1.2 if you have an 80 GB GPU: better on all of it.

## Live end of turn

**LiveKit [eot-bench](https://github.com/livekit/eot-bench)** (validation set, official metrics, eot-bench audio not
in our training data). False cut-offs when the agent may wait at most 300 / 600 ms (lower is better):

| | English | Chinese |
|---|---:|---:|
| **4B-Para-LiveTurn, plugin default with the agent's previous message** (full eot-bench run) | **25.5 / 12.3%** | **38.8 / 12.0%** |
| 4B-Para-LiveTurn, audio only (fast mode) | 25.5 / 12.8% | 39.6 / 13.2% |
| DuplexJev-4B-Para v1.1, audio only (fast mode) | 46.4 / 17.7% | 48.5 / 15.6% |
| DuplexJev-32B-Para v1.2, plugin default (full run) | 20.0 / 9.4% | 37.7 / 12.2% |
| Smart Turn v3.2 | 35.2 / 14.8% | 42.9 / 13.2% |
| LiveKit Turn Detector v1 | 9.9 / 4.5% | 20.6 / 8.7% |

Plugin default: the turn question, P(finished) + P(backchannel), with `The assistant had just said: "..."` before the
audio (the plugins add it from the agent's last message; gateway `duplexjev>=0.6`). Fast mode asks once per pause, at
the 0.2 s score point. Mean wait at ≤5% false cut-offs: English 954 ms (Smart Turn v3.2 1051), Chinese 908 ms (959).

**Pipecat [Smart Turn v3.2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/pipecat-ai/smart-turn-data-v3.2-test) test set**
(accuracy at 0.5, P(finished)): English 93.3% (4B-Para v1.1 67.9%; Smart Turn v3.2 itself 94.7%), Chinese 89.6%
(78.9%; 90.5%). In-distribution: the Smart Turn v3.2 *training* set is in this model's training data.

Easy-Turn test (800, in-domain): 92.0 (4B-Para v1.1 91.0).

## Accents (new)

Held-out speakers of the training corpora (VCTK, English Dialects, EdAcc, common-accent, KeSpeech):

| | 4B-Para v1.1 | **LiveTurn** |
|---|---:|---:|
| English accent, 4-way (19 accents) | 36.5 | **47.9** |
| English region within England, 3-way | 21.4 | **84.4** |
| standard Mandarin or not | 13.4 | **83.5** |
| Mandarin dialect region, 4-way | 30.4 | **39.8** |

Same corpora, different speakers, so these are in-distribution numbers. For DuplexJev-32B-Para v1.2, the Mandarin
judgments held up on unseen corpora and the English accent ones did not (read speech, Speech Accent Archive): do not
rely on English accent answers.

## What it costs

| | 4B-Para v1.1 | **LiveTurn** |
|---|---:|---:|
| qa100 / ZJU-ML | 77 / 58 | 76 / 62 |
| gender / emotion | 89.3 / 90.0 | 89.5 / 90.5 |
| VoiceBench OBQA / MMSU | 55.2 / 42.1 | **49.5 / 39.0** |
| stress: DEBATE meaning / StressTest / StressPresso | 89.9 / 81.2 / 84.2 | **84.9 / 77.5 / 78.2** |
| which word is stressed, zh / en | 90.6 / 92.0 | 86.9 / 86.1 |
| non-verbal sound, VocalSound / NonVerbalSpeech-38K (acc.) | 96.9 / 90.3 | **91.2** / 87.7 |
| speaking style, EARS | 66.8 | 67.7 |

Paper protocol (single-token readout, PyTorch). Through vLLM with `duplexjev-vllm` in the client wording: qa100 78, ZJU-ML 52, gender 88.4, emotion 89.6, Easy-Turn 92.1 (4B-Para v1.1: 76, 51, 87.4, 87.9, 91.4).

## Serve with vLLM

```bash
pip install "vllm[audio]>=0.29" duplexjev-vllm "duplexjev[server]>=0.6"
vllm serve adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B-Para-LiveTurn --max-model-len 4096 --port 8000 &
duplexjev gateway --vllm http://localhost:8000/v1 --port 8420 --rate 1000000
```

Then point the LiveKit or Pipecat plugin at `http://localhost:8420` and give it the agent's previous message
(`detector.attach(session)` in LiveKit, `DuplexJevContextTracker` in Pipecat). Decision prompts are the same as for

# Pocket TTS Japanese

Japanese models for [Pocket TTS](https://github.com/kyutai-labs/pocket-tts) (Kyutai), fine-tuned
from the English 24-layer model with the official training code. Code, training recipe and the
full log of results: [github.com/takuma104/pocket-tts-ja](https://github.com/takuma104/pocket-tts-ja).

- Runs with the **stock `pocket-tts` package** (3.3.0 or later), on CPU, with no code changes.
- Takes **plain Japanese text** (kanji and kana as written). There is no G2P front end; the model
  reads the kanji itself.
- **Zero-shot voice cloning** from a few seconds of reference audio, as in the original.

| Model | Config | FlowLM | Parameters (with the codec) | File |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|
| `japanese` | `japanese.yaml` | 6 layers | 110M | 219 MB |
| `japanese_24l` | `japanese_24l.yaml` | 24 layers | 336M | 1.3 GB |

日本語の概要: Kyutai の Pocket TTS を日本語にファインチューニングしたモデルです。公式の `pocket-tts`
（3.3.0 以降）にそのまま読み込め、CPU で動きます。入力は漢字かな交じりの文で、読みはモデルが決めます
（G2P は使いません）。数秒の参照音声で声を指定します。ウェイトは CC BY-NC 4.0（非商用）です。
コーデック（Mimi）のデコーダーは日本語音声で調整したものです（元のデコーダーの初回版は下記のコミットで使えます）。

## Usage

```bash
uvx pocket-tts generate --config hf://takuma104/pocket-tts-ja/japanese.yaml \
    --voice prompt.wav --text "こんにちは。今日はいい天気ですね。"
```

```python
from pocket_tts import TTSModel

model = TTSModel.load_model(config="hf://takuma104/pocket-tts-ja/japanese.yaml")
voice = model.get_state_for_audio_prompt("prompt.wav")
audio = model.generate_audio(voice, "こんにちは。今日はいい天気ですね。")  # 24 kHz, torch.Tensor
```

- `--voice` is a recording of the voice to clone (a few seconds of clean speech). Without it the
  CLI clones its default voice (alba, an English speaker), which reads Japanese as well (JSUT
  Kana-CER 1.80%, against 2.15% with the JVS prompts). The pre-made voices cannot be selected by
  name (`--voice alba`): they are embeddings computed with the official weights.
- The config sets the sampling temperature to 0.3, the value every number below was measured
  with. Classifier-free guidance (scale 2.0) is distilled into the weights.
- Use `japanese_24l.yaml` for the 24-layer model.
- To keep a fixed version, add a commit hash: `hf://takuma104/pocket-tts-ja/japanese.yaml@<commit>`.
  The first release (same language models, original Mimi decoder) is
  `@ca9b00950babd912554d7de895761f4db1782b5f`.

## Results

All numbers are from generated audio transcribed by an ASR model, with speakers of the JVS corpus
(never trained on) as voice prompts, temperature 0.3, one LSD step.

**Kanji reading: [JKYB-Parakeet](https://github.com/Parakeet-Inc/Joyo-Kanji-Yomi-Benchmark-Parakeet-Edition)**,
all 13,536 sentences, official TTS protocol (kana-whisper). Accuracy is the share of sentences
whose target word is read correctly.

| Model | Prompts: 4 JVS speakers in rotation | Prompt: jvs001 |
|---|---:|---:|
| `japanese` | **94.75%** | **94.84%** |
| `japanese_24l` | 94.32% | 94.49% |
| *First release (original Mimi decoder):* `japanese` | 94.15% | 94.73% |
| *First release:* `japanese_24l` | 93.31% | 94.06% |
| *Original Mimi decoder:* 24-layer teacher before the guidance was distilled (CFG 2.0, not released) | 92.97% | 93.68% |

For reference, with the jvs001 prompt
[Irodori-TTS-v4.1-Small](https://huggingface.co/Aratako/Irodori-TTS-v4.1-Small) scores 94.0% and
[Irodori-TTS-v4.1-Small-Yomi](https://huggingface.co/takuma104/Irodori-TTS-v4.1-Small-Yomi), which
synthesized part of the training data, 95.7%.

**Other sets**, `japanese` with the stock package on CPU (the released bfloat16 file) next to the
GPU evaluation of the same checkpoint:

| Set | Metric | GPU | Stock package, CPU |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| JKYB-mini (1,500 sentences) | accuracy | 95.1% | 95.3% |
| Aozora Bunko ruby (1,000 sentences) | target reading accuracy | 71.3% | |
| JSUT (1,000 sentences) | Kana-CER | 2.28% | 2.15% |
| JVS zero-shot (5 male + 5 female speakers, 10 sentences each) | Kana-CER | 2.32% | 1.70% |
| JVS zero-shot | similarity to the speaker's recording of the same sentence (ECAPA) | 0.577 | 0.575 |
| Short texts (172 texts of 2–8 tokens) | did not stop / extra speech | 0 / 1 | 1 / 1 |

`japanese_24l` is at the same level on these sets (GPU: JKYB-mini 94.5%, Aozora Bunko 71.2%, JSUT
2.28%, JVS 2.13% / 0.586, short texts 0 / 1; stock package on CPU: JKYB-mini 94.7%, JSUT 2.20%,
JVS 1.80% / 0.586, short texts 1 / 3). The 6-layer model reads at least as well as the
24-layer one, so `japanese` is the one to use unless the rarer failure to stop (see Limitations) matters.

## Training

1. A Japanese SentencePiece model with 4,000 pieces replaces the English tokenizer; the text
   embedding is re-initialized. The codec (Mimi) stays frozen while the language model is trained.
2. The 24-layer teacher starts from the English 24-layer model and is trained for 700k steps
   (LSD objective, the voice prompt is another utterance of the same speaker).
3. Natural speech contains few of the rarer kanji readings, so sentences rich in them were
   synthesized with Irodori-TTS-v4.1-Small-Yomi in about 3,000 voices and kept only when an ASR
   model confirmed the reading. The words were chosen without the JKYB keys, and JKYB sentences
   and near duplicates were excluded.
4. Guidance at scale 2.0 is distilled into the weights: into a copy of the 24-layer model
   (`japanese_24l`) and into a 6-layer student initialized from the teacher's layers 0, 1, 2, 21,
   22 and 23 (`japanese`).
5. The decoder of the codec (10M parameters) is fine-tuned on Japanese speech for 90k steps
   (multi-scale mel loss, MPD and MS-STFT discriminators, and a loss on the batch-averaged
   spectrum against the tonal artifacts locked to the decoder's upsampling strides), on clips of
   up to 8 seconds: 182 hours of the synthetic speech and 60 hours of high-bitrate Emilia. In the
   last 10k steps these losses see only the band below 4 kHz, and above it the output is held at
   the level of the original decoder: raised to the level of the recordings, that band was noise
   in voiced speech and audible as a hiss. The encoder is untouched, so latents and voice prompts
   are those of the original Mimi; only the decoder weights inside `model.safetensors` differ
   from the first release.

| Training data | Hours | License |
|---|---:|---|
| [Emilia](https://huggingface.co/datasets/amphion/Emilia-Dataset) Japanese (Emilia and Emilia-YODAS), filtered and re-checked by ASR | 1,531 | CC BY-NC 4.0 / CC BY 4.0 |
| The same clips with a changed gain | 227 | |
| Synthetic speech from Irodori-TTS, readings confirmed by ASR | 828 | text: CC BY-SA and public domain |

ReazonSpeech is not used. JVS and JSUT are used for evaluation only.

## Limitations

- About 5 to 6% of the JKYB sentences are still misread, mostly rare readings and words from the
  appendix of the Joyo kanji table (jukujikun, 89% correct). Numbers, counters and Latin letters
  were not evaluated separately.
- In 0.1 to 0.3% of the JKYB sentences `japanese` does not end the utterance and keeps generating
  up to the length limit (`japanese_24l`: 0.02 to 0.09%).
- Reading accuracy and speaker similarity depend on the voice prompt.
- Real Japanese recordings still lose clarity when they pass through the codec (Kana-CER of JVS
  recordings: 3.3% as recorded, 4.7% through Mimi with the fine-tuned decoder; 5.4% with the
  original decoder). Above 4 kHz the output is as quiet as the original decoder's, 6 to 8 dB
  below the recordings in voiced speech.

## Prohibited use

The prohibited uses of the original Pocket TTS apply: use of the model must comply with all
applicable laws and regulations and must not result in, involve, or facilitate any illegal,
harmful, deceptive, fraudulent, or unauthorized activity. Prohibited uses include, without
limitation, voice impersonation or cloning without explicit and lawful consent; misinformation,

content as genuine recordings of real people or events); and the generation of unlawful, harmful,

([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06926)).

Thanks to Kyutai for Pocket TTS and its training code, to the authors of
[Emilia](https://huggingface.co/datasets/amphion/Emilia-Dataset),
[Irodori-TTS](https://huggingface.co/Aratako/Irodori-TTS-v4.1-Small) (Aratako),
[JKYB-Parakeet](https://github.com/Parakeet-Inc/Joyo-Kanji-Yomi-Benchmark-Parakeet-Edition) and the

# Drama 3 MLX 4-bit

**Built with Fish Audio.**

[Fish Audio Drama 3](https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3) converted for [mlx-audio](https://github.com/Blaizzy/mlx-audio) on Apple Silicon. This is an unofficial community conversion; Fish Audio did not release or endorse it.

- routed experts: 4-bit, dequantized from the block-FP8 release
- dense projections and audio tower: 8-bit
- 22 GB on disk, about 26 GB peak memory while generating

## Usage

Drama 3 support is in review in mlx-audio ([#1018](https://github.com/Blaizzy/mlx-audio/pull/1018)). Until it is merged, install from the PR branch:

```bash
pip install "mlx-audio @ git+https://github.com/stickerdaniel/mlx-audio@fish-drama3"
```

```python
from mlx_audio.tts.utils import load_model

model = load_model("mlx-community/fish-audio-drama-3-4bit")

for result in model.generate(
    text="[sighs] Fine. If we miss it, it's on you.",
    ref_audio="reference.wav",
    ref_text="Transcript of the reference clip.",
    stream=True,
    first_chunk_frames=4,
):
    print(result.audio.shape)  # 44.1 kHz chunks
```

```bash
python -m mlx_audio.tts.generate --model mlx-community/fish-audio-drama-3-4bit \
    --text "[sighs] Fine. If we miss it, it's on you." \
    --ref_audio reference.wav --ref_text "Transcript of the reference clip." \
    --temperature 0.7 --top_p 0.7 --top_k 30
```

Speaker tags (`<|speaker:0|>` to `<|speaker:15|>`), multiple references and streaming are described in the [model docs](https://github.com/stickerdaniel/mlx-audio/blob/fish-drama3/docs/models/tts/fish-drama3.md).

## Quality and speed

On an M3 Max:

- 22 ms per frame (46 ms of audio), about 2x real time
- first streamed audio in 160 to 200 ms once a voice is cached
- teacher-forced against the PyTorch reference: backbone hidden cosine 0.995, semantic top-1 86%

## Conversion

Made with mlx-audio's converter:

```bash
python -m mlx_audio.tts.models.fish_drama3.convert --src drama-3 --dst drama-3-mlx-4bit \
    --expert-bits 4 --dense-bits 8 --tower-bits 8
```

The unquantized weights are at [mlx-community/fish-audio-drama-3-bf16](https://huggingface.co/mlx-community/fish-audio-drama-3-bf16).

`NOTICE` lists every change to the original weights.

# WAXAL VoxCPM2 — 28-Language African TTS

A full fine-tune of [VoxCPM2](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/VoxCPM2) (2B params, tokenizer-free, diffusion-AR TTS with voice cloning) on **28 African languages**, produced by the [WAXAL](https://huggingface.co/waxal-benchmarking) project at [LyngualLabs](https://lynguallabs.org).

This is a research checkpoint. It is not production-polished — see **Known Limitations** below before using it for anything beyond experimentation.

## Languages

VoxCPM2 has no built-in mechanism for specifying language at inference — the base model infers pronunciation purely from text orthography. We added one: a dedicated `<lang:XX>` tag per language, registered as a real token in the tokenizer and resized into the text embedding table (mean-initialized, then learned during fine-tuning). **The tag is mandatory** — always prepend it to the text you want synthesized, e.g.:

```
<lang:yo> Ẹ káàárọ̀! Báwo ni oorun rí lálẹ́ àná?
```

| Language | Tag | Raw hours | Hours after resampling |
|---|---|---|---|
| Yoruba | `<lang:yo>` | 1038.7 | 602.4 |
| Swahili | `<lang:sw>` | 1004.1 | 592.3 |
| Kinyarwanda | `<lang:rw>` | 989.9 | 588.1 |
| Igbo | `<lang:ig>` | 930.2 | 570.1 |
| Hausa | `<lang:ha>` | 682.6 | 488.3 |
| Wolaytta | `<lang:wal>` | 196.6 | 262.1 |
| Dholuo | `<lang:luo>` | 191.5 | 258.7 |
| Amharic | `<lang:am>` | 189.2 | 257.1 |
| Oromo | `<lang:om>` | 189.2 | 257.1 |
| Sidama | `<lang:sid>` | 188.2 | 256.4 |
| Tigrinya | `<lang:tig>` | 180.0 | 250.8 |
| Kikuyu | `<lang:kik>` | 185.8 | 254.8 |
| Kalenjin | `<lang:kal>` | 153.2 | 231.3 |
| Malagasy | `<lang:mlg>` | 179.8 | 250.6 |
| Luganda | `<lang:lug>` | 111.4 | 197.3 |
| Dagaare | `<lang:dagr>` | 104.3 | 190.9 |
| Somali | `<lang:som>` | 103.2 | 189.9 |
| Ewe | `<lang:ewe>` | 103.1 | 189.8 |
| Ikposo | `<lang:ikp>` | 102.6 | 189.3 |
| Wolof | `<lang:wol>` | 101.3 | 188.1 |
| Dagbani | `<lang:dagb>` | 96.3 | 183.4 |
| Maasai | `<lang:maa>` | 83.7 | 171.0 |
| Shona | `<lang:sna>` | 83.7 | 171.0 |
| Akan | `<lang:aka>` | 75.4 | 162.3 |
| Nyankole | `<lang:nya>` | 48.8 | 130.6 |
| Masaaba | `<lang:mas>` | 42.7 | 122.1 |
| Lusoga | `<lang:lus>` | 39.0 | 116.7 |
| Acholi | `<lang:ach>` | 29.7 | 101.9 |

Source data: the [AfroNet](https://huggingface.co/Professor) speech collection (`Professor/<language>-speech-data`), 7,424 raw hours total.

## Training

- **Base**: `openbmb/VoxCPM2`, with 28 new `<lang:XX>` tokens added and the text embedding table resized (mean-initialized rows) before any fine-tuning started — this is an independent run from scratch, not built on top of any earlier narrower fine-tune.
- **Mode**: full fine-tuning (all parameters trainable except the frozen AudioVAE codec).
- **Data balancing**: the 28 languages range 35x in size (1038.7h Yoruba vs. 29.7h Acholi). Naive concatenation would starve the smallest languages; full equalization would cause heavy repetition/overfitting on them. We used **sqrt-temperature resampling** (weight ∝ √hours, renormalized to preserve total volume) — a standard middle-ground technique from multilingual ASR/TTS training. This downsamples the biggest languages to ~58–97% of their raw hours and upsamples the smallest to ~1.4–3.4x, via a combination of subsampling and controlled repetition.
- **Scale**: 2,929,563 training rows (clips) after resampling, 9,450 held-out validation rows.
- **Steps**: 44,000 steps (~0.99 epoch over the resampled training set), batch size 3 × grad-accum 11 × 2 GPUs (effective batch 66).
- **Hardware**: 2× NVIDIA H200, via `torchrun` DDP.
- **Learning rate**: 1e-5, 100 warmup steps.

## Usage

```python
from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download
from voxcpm import VoxCPM
import soundfile as sf

model_dir = snapshot_download("waxal-benchmarking/voxcpm2-multilang28-full")
model = VoxCPM.from_pretrained(model_dir, load_denoiser=False, optimize=False)

wav = model.generate(
    text="<lang:yo> Ẹ káàárọ̀! Báwo ni oorun rí lálẹ́ àná?",
    cfg_value=2.0,
    inference_timesteps=22,
)
sf.write("out.wav", wav, model.tts_model.sample_rate)
```

`optimize=False` is required — `torch.compile` (the default optimization path) conflicts with some inference environments (e.g. HF ZeroGPU Spaces); disabling it costs some speed but avoids crashes.

Voice cloning works the same way as base VoxCPM2 — pass `prompt_wav_path` and `prompt_text` (the literal transcript of what's spoken in the reference clip) alongside the tagged `text`.

Try it live: **[WAXAL VoxCPM Multilingual Demo Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Professor/voxcpm-multilingual28-demo)**.

## Evaluation

We built an automated evaluation pipeline rather than relying on casual listening, using:
- **ASR-based CER** (Character Error Rate) via Meta's [Omnilingual ASR](https://github.com/facebookresearch/omnilingual-asr) (`omniASR_CTC_7B`, ~1,600-language coverage, verified against this model's own supported-language table — not assumed), comparing transcriptions of generated speech against the ground-truth input text.
- The **same ASR run on real human recordings** of the same held-out text, as a per-language noise floor — several of these languages get nontrivial CER even on real speech (e.g. Fante in an earlier AfroNet pilot scored CER 0.49–0.57 on *real* recordings), so a raw TTS CER number is meaningless without that baseline.
- **DNSMOS** (no-reference naturalness proxy). Caveat: DNSMOS is trained on English/high-resource-language listener ratings, so treat these scores as *relative* (comparing our own languages/checkpoints) rather than *absolute*.

Pilot results (5 held-out validation clips per language, no reference voice):

| Metric | Result |
|---|---|
| DNSMOS (naturalness) | 2.78–3.41 across all 28 languages, no outliers |
| Generated-speech CER | Usually *lower* than real-recording CER for the same ASR (e.g. Swahili: 0.028 generated vs. 0.013 real; Hausa: 0.044 vs. 0.113) — generated audio is clean and consistent, so it's often at least as ASR-decodable as noisy real recordings |
| **Non-terminating generation** | A measurable failure mode: in a 5-clip-per-language sample, Malagasy, Sidama, and Somali hit an apparent generation-length ceiling in 3/5 clips; Shona and Swahili in 2/5; several others in 1/5. Confirmed as genuine overrun (not just naturally long sentences) by comparing generated duration against the real recording's duration for the same text. |

The non-terminating-generation issue doesn't cleanly correlate with raw data size — Swahili (one of the largest languages here) is affected while several much smaller languages (Hausa, Acholi, Dagbani, Wolof) show none. It's an open issue, not yet root-caused.

## Known Limitations

- **Voice-design and cross-lingual flexibility are likely reduced.** Earlier narrow single-language full fine-tunes on this same base model showed that full-FT on read-speech-only data degrades the base model's text-prompted style/voice-design control and non-trained-language generation. This 28-language run is far more linguistically diverse than those single-language runs, which should help, but it is still exclusively plain narration-style audio — we have not verified how much voice-design capability survives.
- **Non-terminating generation** (see Evaluation) affects a meaningful minority of generations, worse for some languages (Malagasy, Sidama, Somali) than others.
- **Translation/transcript quality varies by language** in our own test tooling — some of the lowest-resource languages here (Wolaytta, Sidama in particular) have had machine-translated test sentences that looked suspect on inspection; this is a tooling caveat about our *test sentences*, not necessarily the model.
- Language coverage via Omnilingual ASR for evaluation purposes was spot-checked, not independently verified for linguistic accuracy of every transcription.

## Related

- [`waxal-benchmarking/voxcpm2-multilang10-full`](https://huggingface.co/waxal-benchmarking/voxcpm2-multilang10-full) — an earlier, independent fine-tune on just the 10 highest-resource languages from the same collection (Yoruba, Swahili, Kinyarwanda, Igbo, Hausa, Wolaytta, Dholuo, Amharic, Oromo, Sidama), trained the same way.
- [AfroNet speech collection](https://huggingface.co/Professor) — the source training data.
